## 1. The question, frozen

The title names it and the closing line fixes it: **what were "the true facts" of the death at Stoke Moran — what was "the speckled band," and what killed Julia Stoner and Dr. Grimesby Roylott?** Range: the middle bedroom of the inhabited wing, two deaths two years apart. Kind: chiefly **backward** — what can be read off the clues — with a causal mechanism underneath.

## 2. Jobs and parts

**Jobs, each as a contrast.** *Given by the story:* (J1) she died in a room sealed from within, with no wound and no poison found — and not of a cause the coroner could name; (J2) a low whistle about three in the morning, on several nights; (J3) the dying words, "the speckled band"; (J4) a metallic clang; (J5) Julia smelled Roylott's cigar from her room; (J6) a dummy bell-rope, a ventilator into the next room, and a bed clamped to the floor, all fitted about the same time; (J7) a saucer of milk and a looped whip-lash in his room; (J8) both attacks fall when a marriage is pending; (J9) the plotter died, not the intended victim. *Added by me:* (J10) why did no one else in the house ever get bitten?

**Parts, in Holmes's words:** the will-motive; "a swamp adder — the deadliest snake in India"; the ventilator "which does not ventilate"; the dummy rope "as a bridge"; the clamped bed; training with milk and recall by whistle; standing on the worn chair to reach the hole; the clang as the safe door; the band as the snake; the looped lash; the two punctures and the untraceable poison.

## 3. Part by part

| The clang = the safe door | **Two routes** — the safe door, or the shutter-bar falling. Holmes named both |
| "The speckled band" = the snake on the head | **Held** — by J3 |

| The looped lash | **Held** — by "how did he handle the snake without being bitten" (and used on it at the end) |
| Two tiny punctures on the body | **Held if** — it rests on the coroner having missed them |
| A poison no chemical test can find | **Borrowed** — from general lore about Indian snake venom, not tested here |
| "When a doctor does go wrong he is the first of criminals" | **Idle** — colour; no job turns on it |
| The gipsies; the cheetah and baboon as suspects | **Idle** here — parts of Holmes's first, discarded theory |

**Change list:** the claim covers a sleeper in the clamped bed, at night, with Roylott in the next room. It openly leaves out every other room and any bed moved elsewhere — and that limit carries its reason inside it (only that bed sits under the hole).

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** It passes unusually well, because the story performs the flip: the same mechanism bit the plotter instead of the intended victim, with no change to any part. A person-neutral cause is hard to vary. The line "sooner or later she must fall a victim" is a **catch-all** for nights with no bite; it is allowed because it carries a gauge — the whistle, the milk, the nightly trials.

**Direction.** The mechanism is causal: put the snake in and the death follows; show the death and no safe appears. But the **motive is read backwards off the will** — an identification, answering "what can we tell," not "what produced." Worth saying which question each part answers.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** Partly. "The deadliest snake in India" and "a poison no test can find" quietly install the conclusion. The rest is produced — he deduced the ventilator from the cigar smell before he ever saw it.

**Pull.** J1 ("sealed from within") and "a killer entered" pull against each other. The line is drawn at the size of the hole: too small for a man, wide enough for a snake. A hole too narrow even for that snake, or a snake too fat for the hole, would show the line was wrong. Second pull: a £250 saving against the risk of murder — the line rests on "a clever and ruthless man with an Eastern training," which is itself a doubtful job.

**Rivals.** The band of gipsies and death-by-fright each do fewer jobs: neither puts a killer inside a locked room, and both leave the rope, the ventilator, the milk and the clamped bed idle. The sealed room separates them — so they are not the same explanation here. (The extra job J10 kills the gipsy rival again: the gipsies camped every night, yet nobody else died.)

**Where the parts came from.** The mechanism and the will-motive are **built** — worked out with the case in view, then put to the test. The "sealed room" is **given** by the coroner. The species and the venom are **asserted**, backed only by general lore.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

1. **Measure the snake against the hole.** The ventilator is the single load-bearing part — the only thing that lets "sealed from within" and "something got in" both be true. Give it a gauge: an opening wider than the snake's girth, a rope it can grip. That turns "the deadliest snake in India" from a loose label into a held part.
2. **Catch the motive out.** It predicts attacks only while a marriage is pending. It survives the two-year lull unchanged, which is a point in its favour; one attack in a marriage-free year would break it.

## 6. What this does not show

Passing is not truth. The story's world is its own, so a tight mechanism inside a fiction says nothing about real snakes or real crimes. And even a hard-to-vary account of *how* the deaths happened is not proof it happened that way — the official inquiry got the right cause (snakebite) and the wrong story ("indiscreetly playing with a dangerous pet"): same outcome, different workings.

## 7. One next step

Settle the loosest part. Recover the snake from the safe and examine the punctures on the body. If the fang-spacing does not match the species, "the swamp adder" breaks — and the held part underneath it survives.
